items.title: Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped u
items.content:
Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene. 
https://t.co/dIYP7B1GlD

items.content:
a16z's Erin Price-Wright says factory technicians can now retool production lines with AI in 20 minutes, a job that used to take an outside integrator 3 months:

"Historically, if you're setting up a line with a lot of automation, you really need to be producing a lot of one single thing. That's how you get the cost down, and how you justify investing in a pretty bespoke manufacturing line."

"But what we're seeing across our portfolio is that manufacturing technicians themselves have the intuition, and now the software tools, to change the economics of producing low-volume, high-mix on the line."

"A manufacturing technician, not necessarily someone with a college degree or who's studied software engineering, can now use these tools to reprogram and reconfigure their lines on the fly, because they understand the manufacturing process."

"Instead of calling a systems integrator, which takes 3 months and hundreds of thousands of dollars to reconfigure a line, you can have a manufacturing engineer use Claude and do that in 20 minutes. That's been a real game changer."

items.content:
a16z's Connor Love and Erin Price-Wright on what startups should take from SpaceX and Tesla, and when building it all yourself actually makes sense:

Connor: "We can look to Elon for a lot of answers here. I mean, it's not a crazy statement to say really the few modern-day companies that have built anything at scale are probably SpaceX and Tesla. And if you look at how Elon and his team have built those businesses, it's been, one, very vertically integrated."

"I take the ideology that you shouldn't vertically integrate everything. I mean, again, if you're building a super exquisite system like a missile that is doing something very unique, you kind of have to because you have to control the exquisiteness. You have to control the cost."

Erin: "SpaceX and Tesla were doing first of their kind. There didn't exist an industrial base in the US to support them, and so they had to build it themselves. I think where there are high-quality suppliers, you should use suppliers."

Connor: "In a lot of ways they had to make those choices because they didn't have any other opportunity. But in the end, it's actually just that mantra of design for manufacturing that now exists within all these systems companies."

items.content:
Brian Schimpf of @AndurilTech on why industrial production is a deterrent in itself, and why technological superiority alone won't win a war:

"These wars are protracted, they are industrial in scale, and if you were to bring it down to one variable, the amount of kilograms that you can throw at each other turns out to probably be the single most important factor."

"I think the technical superiority is a huge advantage. We're not gonna just outproduce China on like dumb ammunition, right? Like that clearly we have to have an edge around our space capabilities, how we can sense, how we can confuse them, how sophisticated our weapons are."

"But I think the part that got so clear outta Ukraine was that industrial production has a deterrence factor... it is critical for winning a conflict."

"When most of the war games with China show that we'd be out of munitions in... like eight days, that's not a deterrence factor really anymore."

"I think the belief for a long time was that [technological superiority] was sufficient, but a low number of really exquisite weapons is not gonna win a conflict."

@SchimpfBrian (September 2025)

items.title: a16z's Connor Love says building for defense is how America builds for everything else, because once you can make the pa
items.content:
a16z's Connor Love says building for defense is how America builds for everything else, because once you can make the parts "to quality and to cost," new markets start to make sense:

"When you build many systems, you also require many subsystems below that. There are really interesting military systems being built today. The corollary: by building towards defense, you also build for a different industry."

"The subsystems that go into some of our military systems are the exact same subsystems that are going to go into the future robotic systems. It's the actuators, the motors, the valves and switches."

"When you can build those to quality and to cost, then all of a sudden other markets that maybe weren't viable make sense... You're going to have this robotic wave that will come in America."

"AI can't turn a wrench yet. They will eventually. And that will be enabled by all that, actuators and switches and subsystems that we built... And we're not going to have to rely on factories in China."

"As you build an industrial base, an industrial base can be used for many things. Down to the component level, I just think we don’t have enough of it in America."

It's good idea to keep an eye on the effort level you're on. Subagents inherit it by default and it can add up fast. /usage also shows where a session's tokens went.

items.title:
Top 5 learnings growing The Rundown to 3.5M total active subscribers and 55%+ open rate:

1. Email is its own platform,
items.content:
Top 5 learnings growing The Rundown to 3.5M total active subscribers and 55%+ open rate:

1. Email is its own platform, treat it like YouTube, Instagram, Twitter

Super readers (open every email, click ads, and stick around for years) genuinely like email as a medium. We have millions of readers who don’t use social media. Best way to acquire them is through other newsletters, referrals, or being the reason they stop using social media.

Barely anyone is building for this audience. I’m more bullish on email than any other platform (long-form YouTube is a close second).

2. The newsletter industry lacks innovation

Look at mobile apps, ecom, edtech. Custom quiz onboarding, a landing page for every ad, hundreds of new creatives a day. Meanwhile most newsletters, including some of the biggest in the world, have a basic landing page and standard onboarding.

We built an onboarding quiz funnel that, at one point, got us close to negative CAC with hundreds of thousands a month in ad spend. That’s what let us scale aggressively and outbid competitors.

With AI coding and platforms like beehiiv, there’s no excuse not to build new experiences for your readers. The opportunity here is wide open :)

3. Newsletter sales is mostly an education problem

We still run social partnerships at a significantly higher CPM than our newsletters, yet the newsletters convert better and get way more clicks.

A lot of advertisers don’t understand newsletters as they do with influencer marketing, so at scale it becomes an education game. 

Once advertisers get it, they stay. We’ve been booked out at multiple ads a day for the last 3 years, months in advance.

4. Stay lean, fast, aggressive

Other newsletters have built large sales and content teams. I think it’s better to stay small and pay high-quality people to do very good work.

Revenue can increase with more employees, but the opportunity cost of not moving fast in the AI era is a long-term net negative. 

For example, we constantly test new growth experiments and new forms of media. Most don’t work and that’s fine. The point is we can pivot the same day because we're lean.

5. Lastly, don’t listen to people who say email is dead or that you shouldn’t run paid ads. That’s ignorance and lowkey skill issue.

For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :

It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!

It can talk(kinda)

You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.

If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

You are not behind (yet). 

Here's how to learn Claude in 3 mins:

> Use 'Medium' effort. Never Max. 
> Low for grammar, high for one big prompt.
> Use '/setup' command for Claude to onboard you.
> Get $100/plan for 5× the usage of the $20 plan.
> Give "goal" in the prompt, not "HOW"
> Paste my specific prompt into Claude to start a new chat: https://t.co/NYWCbdG35N.
> Save your one free reset for a bad day.
> Use Opus 5.5 in every chat. Never Fable.
> Never switch models mid-chat.
> Never go back to an old chat.
> Ask for a 10-line summary & paste it in a new one.
> End questions with "No web search. No files."
> Plan your deck in text first. Ask for the file last.
> Highlight the part to fix, click "Edit with Claude".
> Load your apps on demand (+ → Connectors → Tool access)
> Paste Anthropic's 2 sentences into Settings → General → Instructions
> Crop every screenshot. Turn every PDF into text
> Pause every scheduled task you don't read.
> Start every task with "Ask me questions before you start."
> Put all your asks in one message.
> Speak your prompts. I use Wispr Flow. 
> Never correct Claude. Edit your prompt or start. 
> One topic per chat.
> Keep your instructions under 2,000 words.
> Upload files you reuse once, in a Project.

items.title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents
items.content:
Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic (https://simantic.com). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware.

Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes.

We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago.

To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds.

What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit.

Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ

Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars.

We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time.

Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode (https://github.com/renode/renode) and QEMU (https://www.qemu.org/), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this.

1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast.

2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself.

3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. Renode is an emulator at the core, but our users, especially those who are building systems where timing accuracy is crucial did not find the accuracy good enough to validate their firmware.

Because of these issues, we made our own simulation engine from scratch, fully written in Rust.

- Our simulation is focused on accuracy. Open source frameworks often focus on expandability and developer experience, which means there were a lot of tradeoffs made to prioritize a breadth of models rather than going deep into a set of select models.

- We have our own hardware validation rigs running 24/7 to ensure our simulation models are as close to real world hardware as possible, and any gaps are detected and fixed as soon as we can. It currently looks like devboards connected to a Saleae Logic MSO and a SWD bus, controlled by a Linux PC, running Claude 24/7 just finding these gaps.

Our cloud-hosted simulator is available to use right now! We also provide a native binary with our developer plan licenses that let you run your firmware on your machines locally without any limitations.

Check it out at https://simantic.com/cloud-sim, and you can start using our AI firmware reviewer bot in your own Github repos here: https://simantic.com/dashboard/simantic-bot.

We currently have support for some models of the STM32F0, F4, H7 series MCUs, ESP32-S3/C3, and RP2040, but we’re constantly working to release new models every week, and improve our existing ones.

Thank you, and if you have any questions, feel free to send us an email at founders@simantic.dev

One of the best businesses to run with AI is a leak fix for boring local companies.

A boring company already pays for ads to get traffic to its website. You turn that traffic into more calls and more booked jobs.

4) Combine it with the best direct-to-consumer funnel and ad strategies.

5) Sell one result: more calls from the traffic that they pay for now.

6) Measure the return and show it to the owner.

Step 6 works only after step 1. Lawn maintenance and restaurants have a low ticket. A plumbing job can cost thousands of dollars, and the homeowner needs the repair that day.

Two weeks ago, water came through my ceiling. That day, I paid approximately $2,000 for water restoration.
When you can show the return, the owner will keep you.

Pick the niche, find the ad spend, then fix the leak.

If you are a Claude freak like me, and you don't know how people are making crazy websites in Claude. Then this post is for you:

If not, you're going to think it's extremely technical & overly complex (even though it is stupid simple).

I can't make it any simpler than this:

Step 1. Pick a website that you wish you'd made.

→ Go to Awwwards to find award-winning websites.
→ Go to Godly .design for design inspiration.
→ Go to OnePageLove .com for single page website

Step 2. Copy my exact prompt from this free guide: https://t.co/JBAhZFLwVf

DO NOT skip this part!!!

Step 3. Create a (free) GitHub account. 

It keeps your website’s code.

It does look technical, but you don't have to do anything technical in it.

Step 4. Now, create a Vercel account. 

→ It publishes your website on the internet.
→ Free Vercel account for personal websites.
→ But get the $20/month plan if you want to push a business website.

Step 5. Go to the Claude desktop app → Code.

→ Pick a new, empty folder on your desktop.
→ Select 'Auto' mode (so Claude won't annoy you to give it permissions to do things).
→ Select Opus 5.5 on medium (quite important)

Step 6. Paste the prompt & replace the link with the website you picked.

"/goal Remake [THE WEBSITE URL YOU CHOSE] with github .com/rubenhassid1/remake until its report says REMAKE COMPLETE, or stop after 100 turns."

Step 7. Let Claude cook. 

It took my Claude about 58 minutes for the award-winning website clone, page by page.

Step 8. Claude must have taken your inspiration website video & pictures (not ideal).

So to replace every picture & video, copy the follow-up prompt from the same guide: https://t.co/JBAhZFLwVf

Add your context by: 

> Telling Claude your company name. 
> What you do. 
> Your brand colors. 
> Where your own photos are.

Claude will remake new pictures in the same shape, light & colors as the original, for your company.

Step 9. The last step has to be: Make it yours.

> Replace the inspiration website text with yours.
> Replace the inspiration website logos with yours.

After doing all of this, I still don’t know how to code. And I do not need to.

Yet I gave Claude one prompt to make 3 websites for my company GPC.

I was impressed with what Claude made with just one prompt, with no edits on my end. Not even ever touching the code.

items.content:
Claudeを本気で使いこなしたい人、AnthropicのGitHubは
見ておいた方がいい。

プロンプトの基礎から、
アプリ開発、
コードレビューの自動化まで。

学習に使える教材やサンプルが
無料で公開されている👇　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　

この7つは順番に触ると理解しやすい。

① prompt-eng-interactive-tutorial
→ Claudeへの「伝え方」を学ぶ

指示の組み立て方、
具体例の渡し方、
回答の精度を高める工夫。

まずは、
欲しい答えを引き出すための土台から。

② claude-cookbooks
→ 実例を動かして使い方をつかむ

RAG、ツール連携、画像の扱い、プロンプトキャッシュなど。
サンプルを動かしながら、自分の用途に合わせて変更していく。

③ claude-quickstarts
→ アプリとして形にする

サポートエージェントやデスクトップ操作などの実装例。
個別の機能が、どう一つのアプリにつながるのかが見えてくる。

④ skills
→ 自分の仕事の進め方を教える

手順やルール、参考資料をSKILL.mdと関連ファイルにまとめる。
毎回説明している作業を、再利用できる形にする。

⑤ claude-agent-sdk-python
→ 自分専用のエージェントを作る

Pythonから、ツールやフックを組み合わせて処理を設計する。
調査、実行、確認までをつなぐ段階へ。

⑥ claude-code
→ コードベースで実際に働かせる

コードを読み、ファイルを編集し、コマンドを実行する。
ここまで学んだことを、日々の開発に落とし込む。

⑦ claude-code-action
→ GitHub上の作業につなげる

PRやIssueを起点に、レビューや修正を支援させる。
設定を整えれば、開発フローの中にClaudeを組み込める。

おすすめは、全部を読み切ろうとするより「自分が毎週やっている作業」を一つ選ぶこと。

レビューでも、調査でも、定型作業でもいい。
学んだ内容をその作業に使うと、必要な知識がつながっていく。

「Claudeに質問できる」から、
「Claudeが働く仕組みを作れる」へ。

この7つを実践につなげるためのプロンプトガイドはこちら 👇 https://t.co/foo5jn9Xzl
